---
title: "Monotonic Clock and `Stopwatch` in .NET"
---

## 1. Two kinds of clocks

Your computer keeps two different kinds of time, and they answer different questions.

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────────┐
│        WALL CLOCK           │      │      MONOTONIC CLOCK        │
│  DateTime.Now / UtcNow      │      │  Stopwatch                  │
├─────────────────────────────┤      ├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Q: "What time is it?"       │      │ Q: "How much time passed?"  │
│ Has meaning: 2026-10-01     │      │ Arbitrary origin (e.g. boot)│
│ Can JUMP forward/backward   │      │ Only moves FORWARD, steadily│
│ Good for: timestamps, logs  │      │ Good for: durations, timeouts│
└─────────────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────────┘
```

A monotonic clock is a counter that only ever increases, at a steady rate. Its raw value means nothing by itself, such as "123,456,789,000 ticks since some unspecified point". Only the difference between two readings is meaningful.

## 2. Why the wall clock is dangerous for measuring time

The wall clock can be changed while your code is running. This happens in several ways:

- NTP sync can correct clock drift by a few ms or seconds.
- A user or admin can manually change the time.
- `DateTime.Now` (local time) shifts by an hour at daylight saving time transitions.
- A VM can resume from a snapshot or pause.

Here is what that looks like:

```
Real time     ──────────────────────────────────────────▶
               start                              end
                 │       (NTP corrects -2s)        │
Wall clock    10:00:00 ─────── 10:00:03 ↘ 10:00:01 ─── 10:00:02
                                                  
  end - start  = 2 s      ❌ (actually took 4 s)
  could even be NEGATIVE  ❌ if the jump is big enough

Monotonic     1000 ────────────────────────────────── 5000 (ms ticks)
  end - start  = 4 s      ✅ unaffected by clock changes
```

So this common pattern is subtly wrong:

```csharp
// ❌ Don't measure durations with the wall clock
var start = DateTime.Now;
DoWork();
var elapsed = DateTime.Now - start;   // may be wrong, even negative
```

## 3. `Stopwatch`: .NET's monotonic, high-resolution timer

`System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch` wraps the operating system's monotonic high-resolution counter:

```
              Stopwatch
                  │
   ┌──────────────┼───────────────────┐
   ▼              ▼                   ▼
Windows        Linux               macOS (your M3)
QueryPerf-     clock_gettime       OS monotonic
Counter()      (CLOCK_MONOTONIC)   counter (nanosecond-scale)
```

### Basic instance usage

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics;

var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();   // create + start

DoWork();

sw.Stop();
Console.WriteLine($"Took {sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds:F3} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"Took {sw.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");   // long, truncated
```

Useful members:

| Member | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Start()` / `Stop()` | Resume / pause accumulating time |
| `Reset()` | Stop and zero |
| `Restart()` | Zero and start again (handy for laps) |
| `Elapsed` | `TimeSpan` (most convenient) |
| `ElapsedMilliseconds` | `long` ms |
| `ElapsedTicks` | Raw counter ticks (see gotcha below) |
| `IsRunning` | Whether it is running |

### Static, allocation-free usage (.NET 7+, preferred in hot paths)

You don't even need an object. Just grab timestamps:

```csharp
long start = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

DoWork();

TimeSpan elapsed = Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start);
Console.WriteLine($"Took {elapsed.TotalMilliseconds:F3} ms");
```

This is great for logging middleware, or anything called millions of times, since `Stopwatch` is a class and `GetTimestamp()` is just a `long`.

## 4. Classic gotcha: two kinds of "ticks"

This trips up many people:

```
Stopwatch.ElapsedTicks   → raw counter ticks, rate = Stopwatch.Frequency (per second)
TimeSpan.Ticks           → always 100 ns units (10,000,000 per second)
```

They are not the same unit unless the frequency happens to be 10 MHz.

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(Stopwatch.Frequency);        // e.g. 1_000_000_000 on macOS (ns)
Console.WriteLine(Stopwatch.IsHighResolution); // True

// ❌ Wrong: treating Stopwatch ticks as TimeSpan ticks
var wrong = new TimeSpan(sw.ElapsedTicks);

// ✅ Right: use Elapsed, or convert manually
var right = sw.Elapsed;
double seconds = (double)sw.ElapsedTicks / Stopwatch.Frequency;
```

Rule of thumb: use `Elapsed` or `GetElapsedTime()` and you'll never hit this.

## 5. Other monotonic options in .NET

| API | Resolution | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Stopwatch` / `GetTimestamp()` | Sub-µs (ns on macOS) | Best general choice |
| `Environment.TickCount64` | ~ms (OS dependent) | Cheap, coarse; good for timeouts |
| `TimeProvider.System.GetTimestamp()` (.NET 8+) | Same as Stopwatch | **Testable** abstraction |

### `TimeProvider`: the clean-architecture way

Since you care about SOLID, this one matters. Hard-coding `Stopwatch` or `DateTime.UtcNow` makes time-dependent code hard to unit test. .NET 8 introduced `TimeProvider`, which you can inject as a dependency:

```csharp
public sealed class RequestTimer(TimeProvider clock)
{
    public TimeSpan Measure(Action action)
    {
        long start = clock.GetTimestamp();          // monotonic
        action();
        return clock.GetElapsedTime(start);
    }
}

// Production
var timer = new RequestTimer(TimeProvider.System);
```

In tests, you inject `FakeTimeProvider` (from the `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` package) and advance time manually with `fake.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))`. There's no real waiting and the tests are deterministic. `TimeProvider` exposes both kinds of clock: `GetUtcNow()` for wall time and `GetTimestamp()` for monotonic time.

## 6. Practical caveats

1. **Not a benchmarking tool.** Wrapping one call in a `Stopwatch` measures JIT compilation, cache warm-up, GC pauses, and so on. For serious micro-benchmarks, use **BenchmarkDotNet**, which handles warm-up, iterations, and statistics.
2. **Not thread-safe.** Don't `Start`/`Stop` one instance from multiple threads. Use per-thread timestamps instead.
3. **Sleep behavior is platform-dependent.** Whether the counter advances while the machine is asleep varies by OS. This rarely matters for in-process timing.
4. **Never use it for "time of day".** The raw value has no calendar meaning. Pair it with `DateTime.UtcNow` if you need both, for example "started at 10:00 UTC, took 3.2 s".

## 7. Summary

```
Need "WHEN did it happen?"     → DateTime.UtcNow / DateTimeOffset.UtcNow  (wall clock)
Need "HOW LONG did it take?"   → Stopwatch.GetTimestamp() + GetElapsedTime (monotonic)
Need it testable / injectable  → TimeProvider
Need rigorous perf numbers     → BenchmarkDotNet
```

A quick experiment to try on your Mac:

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics;

Console.WriteLine($"Frequency: {Stopwatch.Frequency:N0} ticks/s");
Console.WriteLine($"High-res:  {Stopwatch.IsHighResolution}");

long t0 = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();
Thread.Sleep(100);
Console.WriteLine($"Slept ≈ {Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(t0).TotalMilliseconds:F3} ms");
```

You'll notice the sleep is never exactly 100.000 ms. That's OS scheduling, and seeing it is part of the lesson. Next time, we could look at how `CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan)` and `PeriodicTimer` use monotonic time under the hood.
